site.title: Sleeve
site.tagline: Fifty years of Nigerian sound, judged by its cover.
site.intro: A scrolling history of Nigerian music told through its album art, and through the painters, photographers and art directors who made it. Five eras, five visual languages, one crate.

terms.heading: Afrobeat is not Afrobeats
terms.afrobeat: Afrobeat, no s: the genre Fela Kuti built in Lagos at the turn of the 1970s. Long, horn-driven, polyrhythmic songs with jazz, funk, highlife and Yoruba roots, and lyrics that went after the government by name.
terms.afrobeats: Afrobeats, with an s: the broad umbrella, named and popularised in London in the early 2010s, for contemporary Nigerian and West African pop. It borrows from Afrobeat, but it is a much wider sound and a marketing term as much as a genre.

designers.heading: The people behind the sleeve
designers.intro: A cover reaches more people than any single song. These are the painters, photographers and designers whose names are printed on the sleeves in this crate.

people.name: Lemi Ghariokwu
people.style: Dense, hand-painted political illustration: comic-panel compositions, caricatured soldiers and officials, hand-drawn lettering.
people.note: Self-taught, he met Fela in 1974 through the journalist Babatunde Harrison and drew Alagbon Close, the first of 26 covers he made for him. His Soweto-inspired design for Sorrow Tears and Blood was turned down, and the two fell out for eight years. His work was shown at the New Museum in New York in 2003, and The Observer called him the "King of Covers". Thirty years after Zombie, his name is on the sleeve of 2face's debut.

people.name: Remi Olowookere
people.style: Full-colour comic-strip illustration: crowded scenes, explosive bursts and lettering that repeats and changes colour.
people.note: Credited for the artwork on two of Fela's 1975 albums. The gridlocked Lagos street of Confusion, a policeman swallowed by flame-coloured bursts, is among the decade's most energetic sleeves.

people.name: Peter Obe
people.style: Documentary photojournalism, cut out and recombined on the sleeve into satire.
people.note: Peter Obe (1932–2013) rose to chief press photographer at the Daily Times and made his name with daring coverage of the Nigerian civil war, collected in his 1971 photobook Nigeria: A Decade of Crises in Pictures. His agency is credited on two of Fela's mid-seventies sleeves.

people.name: Tunde Kuboye and Femi Osunla
work: Sorrow Tears and Blood (1977), Femi Osunla
people.style: Stage and portrait photography of Fela and Afrika 70.
people.note: The photographers credited on the sleeves of three of Fela's 1977 albums, the year of the raid on Kalakuta. Osunla's stage portrait is the whole front cover of Sorrow Tears and Blood.

people.name: Bruno Tilley
people.style: International art direction: a single striking portrait, colour fields and small, quiet type.
people.note: The designer credited across all three of King Sunny Adé's albums for Island Records, working with the photographers Adrian Boot (Juju Music), Lynn Goldsmith (Synchro System) and Brian Griffin (Aura). His covers introduced jùjú to record shops far from Lagos.

people.name: Biodun Sowunmi
people.style: A framed portrait and script lettering on a pale ground.
people.note: Credited with the artwork of Obey's Austerity, one of the few 1980s jùjú sleeves in this crate to print the name of its maker.

people.name: Kelechi Amadi-Obi
people.style: Glossy, staged celebrity portraiture shaped by a painter's eye for light.
people.note: Born in Owerri in 1969, he qualified as a lawyer, was called to the bar in 1993, then turned to painting and photography. He became one of Nigeria's best-known fashion photographers and in 2010 launched Mania, a fashion magazine. His photograph is the cover of P-Square's Game Over.

people.name: Osa Seven and Seyi Charles George
work: Superstar (2011), Wizkid: artwork (Osa Seven), photography (Seyi Charles George)
people.style: Bright digital pop: light bursts, stars and bold pink type around a styled portrait.
people.note: Credited on the back cover of Wizkid's debut, one of the first covers of the Afrobeats decade to name both its artist and its photographer.

people.name: Chuka Obi
work: Twice as Tall (2020), Burna Boy, album cover design
people.style: Larger-than-life digital painting: a titan striding across a continent.
people.note: Credited with the album cover design on the vinyl edition of Twice as Tall, which won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album: Burna Boy as a giant, boot raised, passing pyramids and West African monuments under a burning sky.

people.name: Lanre Williams (Willy's Art)
people.style: Storybook illustration drawn from comics, 2D cartoons and manga: serious subjects drawn to look as childlike as possible.
people.note: Rema sketched a house burning with a skeleton coming through it, and Williams turned it into the final cover in four to five days. Each symbol stands for part of Rema's story: the skeleton, the rose, the sun, the grave and sword, the swing.

closing.heading: From the Shrine to the streaming tile
paragraphs: In 1977 a Nigerian record sleeve was a placard: a painting you could hold up, aimed at the men in uniform. By the 2020s it is a square shown 60 pixels wide in a playlist and a billboard-sized image at a sold-out arena, and it has to work at both sizes.

What carried across fifty years was the idea that the cover is an argument. Lemi Ghariokwu's crowded panels argued with the state. Today's quieter portraits argue about who gets to be seen, and how. The hand-lettering became a script signature, the collage became a 3D render, and the comic panel became a storybook illustration like Rave & Roses.

The world started paying attention. Lemi Ghariokwu's covers have been exhibited in New York and Britain, Fela's sleeves are reissued and reframed, and a generation of Nigerian illustrators and photographers now art-directs global releases. Fifty years on, the crate is full.

eras.title: Afrobeat and the Revolution
eras.lede: Fela Kuti, Africa 70, and covers painted like front pages.
essay: The 1970s opened with Nigeria emerging from civil war in January 1970 and sliding straight into an oil boom. Petrodollars poured into Lagos, the city swelled, and the country was ruled by soldiers: Yakubu Gowon until 1975, then Murtala Mohammed, then Olusegun Obasanjo. Multinational labels like EMI and Decca pressed records in Lagos, and Lagos nightlife had money to spend.

Fela Ransome-Kuti came home from ten months in Los Angeles in 1969 carrying Black Power politics and a new sound. Afrobeat (no s) welded highlife and jazz to James Brown's funk, with Tony Allen's drumming at its centre and songs that ran a whole LP side. He sang in pidgin so the whole of West Africa could follow, and he named names. By the mid-decade he had dropped "Ransome" for "Anikulapo" and declared his compound, the Kalakuta Republic, independent of the state.

If the songs were editorials, the sleeves were front pages. From 1974 the self-taught painter Lemi Ghariokwu, barely out of his teens, gave Fela's records their look: crowded comic panels, caricatured soldiers and officials, hand-drawn lettering in hot ochres and reds. Around him, graphic artists like Remi Olowookere and photographers like Peter Obe turned the cover into reportage. Each record arrived as an argument you could hold.

The argument had a price. After Zombie mocked the army as mindless automatons, around a thousand soldiers stormed Kalakuta in February 1977. Fela was beaten, the compound was burned, and his mother, the activist Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was thrown from a window and died of her injuries the following year. The records that followed, Sorrow Tears and Blood and No Agreement, carry that confrontation on their sleeves.

spotlight.who: Lemi Ghariokwu, the self-taught Lagos artist who designed 26 covers for Fela between 1974 and the end of the 1980s.
spotlight.what: Fela in a pink shirt, mid-gesture with the microphone, squares up to soldiers blown up to monstrous size and cut into collage fragments: helmets, hands, boots. Scale is the argument. The army is huge, faceless and in pieces, and the one man facing it is whole.
spotlight.why: Zombie was the record the state answered with force. The cover turns the song's mockery of soldiers who march without thinking into a single image you can read from across a market. It is the moment the Nigerian album sleeve stopped being packaging and became protest art.

eras.title: Jùjú, Fújì and Highlife
eras.lede: King Sunny Adé, Ebenezer Obey, Sikiru Ayinde Barrister, Oliver De Coque.
essay: The oil boom ended in debt. When oil prices fell at the start of the 1980s, Shehu Shagari's civilian government rushed an Economic Stabilisation Act through parliament in April 1982, cutting imports and travel allowances, and Ebenezer Obey put the word "Austerity" straight on a record sleeve. A coup at the end of 1983 brought Muhammadu Buhari to power; another in 1985 brought Ibrahim Babangida, whose Structural Adjustment Programme let the naira collapse in a new foreign-exchange market from September 1986. Imported records, pressing materials and nights out all got dearer.

The dance floor still belonged to Yoruba praise music. Jùjú, built on guitars, talking drums and call-and-response, was led by two rival bandleaders: King Sunny Adé and "Chief Commander" Ebenezer Obey, each fronting a large band and turning out several albums a year. Fújì grew from Muslim wéré and ajísáàrí singing and older styles like apala and sakara; its pioneer Sikiru Ayinde Barrister led a 34-member band called the Supreme Fuji Commanders. Highlife held the east, where Oliver De Coque's Igbo guitar band drew on ogene rhythms and Congolese guitar lines.

Jùjú also went abroad. Island Records signed King Sunny Adé to its Mango imprint, and Juju Music (1982) became his first worldwide release, produced by Martin Meissonnier with synthesizers and drum machines layered over the talking drums. The follow-up, Synchro System (1983), earned the first Grammy nomination for a Nigerian artist.

That split produced two cover traditions. At home a sleeve sold the band as an institution: the bandleader in lace or patterned agbada, praise names and titles in heavy outlined type, the tracklist printed straight onto the front. The photographers were rarely credited. For the international releases Island brought in its own designer, Bruno Tilley, and named its photographers on every sleeve.

spotlight.who: Photography by Adrian Boot and design by Bruno Tilley, according to the album's credits. They made it for Island Records' Mango imprint, the label that took King Sunny Adé worldwide.
spotlight.what: Adé's face is set as a high-contrast, posterised portrait, half dissolving into flowing bands of red, gold, green and black. The band name and title sit small at the centre in a quiet serif. There is no line-up in agbada, no painted studio, no praise names: the bandleader becomes a single graphic icon.
spotlight.why: This is how much of the world first met jùjú. Set it beside a Lagos-pressed sleeve of the same years and you see the decade's two cover traditions at once: the full-band studio portrait sold status to a home audience, while this cover sold one face, and a mood, to record shops in London and New York.

fonts.name: Ultra
fonts.role: Display. A fat slab, outlined and drop-shadowed

eras.title: Naija Hip-Hop and the CD Era
eras.lede: 2face Idibia, P-Square, D'banj, Don Jazzy and Mo'Hits, Styl-Plus.
essay: In May 1999 Olusegun Obasanjo was sworn in as president, and Nigeria returned to civilian rule after sixteen years of military government. The new freedom was audible. Private radio had been on air since Ray Power launched in Lagos in 1994, mobile phones arrived when the first GSM networks switched on in August 2001, and pan-African music television, Channel O from 1997 and MTV Base Africa from 2005, put Nigerian videos in front of the whole continent.

A generation raised on American hip-hop and R&B started making it in Nigerian English, pidgin and Yoruba. Groups like the Plantashun Boiz and Styl-Plus set the harmonies. Labels such as Kennis Music and, from the mid-2000s, Don Jazzy and D'banj's Mo' Hits built the stars. The music stayed political: Eedris Abdulkareem's "Jaga Jaga" (2004), a lament about corruption, was banned from radio and attacked by Obasanjo himself.

The money moved through a market. Alaba International Market in Lagos, West Africa's largest electronics market, became the hub where CDs were pressed, copied and sold on to traders across the region, and the capital of Nigerian music piracy. The same networks moved Nollywood's home videos. Piracy was so woven into the trade that bootleg compilations often did the publicity for new artists, who made their money on stage. A hit like 2face's "African Queen" travelled the continent from those stalls.

Covers were made to win a market-stall wall. Early-digital design took over: cut-out portraits on glowing gradients and city skylines, titles in chrome and bevel with lens flares, and stickers printed straight onto the sleeve to plug the hit single. Most designers went uncredited. When a name was printed, it was usually the photographer's.

spotlight.who: Photography by Kelechi Amadi-Obi, according to the album's credits. Amadi-Obi qualified as a lawyer and worked as a painter before becoming one of Nigeria's best-known fashion and celebrity photographers.
spotlight.what: Peter and Paul Okoye in white suits and dark glasses fan a hand of playing cards at the camera while dice fly towards the viewer. A city skyline glows behind them, and "Game Over" is set in chrome bevelled lettering above the Square Records logo.
spotlight.why: Game Over was conceived as a visual album, with a music video for nearly every song, and the sleeve plays like the poster for that film. Released on the twins' own label, it is the CD era's maximalism at full stretch: chrome type, flying dice, a glossy city, all built to stand out on an Alaba wall. It is also one of the few covers of the era with a printed photography credit. A 2008 reissue changed the cover.

fonts.role: Display. Wide and extended, made for chrome and bevel

eras.title: Afrobeats Rises
eras.lede: Wizkid, Davido, Burna Boy, Tiwa Savage, Olamide.
essay: The word "Afrobeats" belongs to the 2010s. In April 2011 the London DJ Abrantee launched the first radio show branded "Afrobeats" on Choice FM, and the name stuck as an umbrella for the new Nigerian and Ghanaian pop filling the city's club nights. It borrowed Fela's genre name but not his form: these were three-minute songs built for the dance floor and the phone. Fela's Afrobeat and this Afrobeats are related, but they are not the same thing.

The diaspora turned the scene into an export. Nigerian and Ghanaian communities in London, Houston and Toronto booked the artists, played the records and carried them onto mainstream radio. D'banj's "Oliver Twist" entered the UK chart at number nine in May 2012, and Wizkid's feature on Drake's "One Dance" (2016) put a Lagos voice at number one in Britain and America.

The CD faded from the centre. Singles broke on YouTube and blogs, albums went up on iTunes, and caller tunes, which MTN launched in 2008, paid Nigerian artists billions of naira in royalties. Music videos became the main stage, and with them came stylists, choreographers and directors such as Clarence Peters. By the end of the decade streaming apps built for African phones, such as Boomplay, were growing, and the next era would belong to them.

Covers caught up with the videos. The bevelled chrome gave way to fashion-editorial portraits on seamless paper, flat colour blocking and confident sans wordmarks, with styling treated as part of the statement. Tiwa Savage's triple portrait in white and Yemi Alade crowned in gold are both portraits meant to work as images on their own. Back covers began crediting the people who made them: Wizkid's Superstar names its photographer and its artwork designer.

spotlight.who: Photography by Seyi Charles George and album artwork by Osa Seven, both credited on the album's back cover.
spotlight.what: Wizkid in a red cap and sunglasses with his name across the lenses, against a burst of rainbow light rays and stars. "Superstar" is set in bold pink and white, with stars knocked into the letters and the Empire Mates label mark in the corner.
spotlight.why: A debut that sells a persona before a song: the name is printed on his glasses and the title is a promise. Its bright digital light-burst sits halfway between the CD era's chrome and the flat editorial covers the decade was heading for. Printed credits for both a photographer and a designer mark the start of the makers being named again.

fonts.name: Archivo
fonts.role: Display. A confident grotesque, wide or condensed on demand

motifs: Flat colour blocking, one or two fields
Fashion-editorial studio portraits

A minimal sans wordmark, often small

Square crops designed for the phone screen

eras.title: Global
eras.lede: Burna Boy, Wizkid, Rema, Tems, Asake, Ayra Starr, and the amapiano crossover.
essay: By 2020, Afrobeats (with an s) was no longer a scene. It was one of the world's pop exports. The CD economy of Lagos markets and their pirated compilations had given way to streaming: Boomplay and Audiomack at home, Spotify arriving in Nigeria in February 2021, and diaspora audiences in London, Houston and Toronto streaming Lagos releases on the same day as Lagos.

The decade opened in turmoil. In October 2020 the #EndSARS protests against police brutality filled Nigerian streets, and Wizkid pushed Made in Lagos back to the end of the month because of them. Burna Boy's Twice as Tall won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album the following spring, and its companion comic was narrated by Benson Idonije, who had once managed Fela. Wizkid and Tems' "Essence" reached the US top ten, Rema's "Calm Down", remixed with Selena Gomez, climbed to number three on the Billboard Hot 100, and South African amapiano bled into Lagos, from Asake's fújì-inflected log drums to Davido's largely amapiano Timeless.

The covers changed scale. A sleeve now has to read as a 60-pixel tile in a playlist, a full-screen phone wallpaper and a billboard. The answer was cinematic restraint: muted grounds, a single figure, fine-art lighting, a handwritten script for a title (Made in Lagos, Born in the Wild, The Year I Turned 21). Alongside that came fully illustrated worlds by young Nigerian artists, like Lanre Williams' storybook Rave & Roses, and digital painting and compositing (Timeless, Twice as Tall).
One thing got harder: credits. Liner notes have dissolved into Instagram captions and press-kit PDFs, and the makers of many 2020s covers are harder to name than the painters of the 1970s.

spotlight.who: Lanre Williams, the illustrator known as Willy's Art, working from Rema's own sketch: a house burning, a skeleton coming through it. The final design took four to five days.
spotlight.what: A cream page with a story scattered across it. Rema is the skeleton running towards the sun with a rose. The burning house is where he wrote the songs ("so hard they can make a house explode"). The grave and sword mark the father and brother he lost. The swing in the clouds points back to his early EPs.
spotlight.why: It refuses the decade's default of the cinematic portrait. Like Lemi Ghariokwu fifty years earlier, it hands the cover to an illustrator and fills it with symbols to decode. Unlike Lemi's, it is weightless and mostly empty, built to read at phone size. It is proof that the Nigerian illustrated sleeve never left; it changed register.

sleeves.title: Roforofo Fight
sleeves.label: Jofabro (Nigerian EMI)
sleeves.artNotes: A stage photograph of Fela mid-song in a white shirt, cut out against pure black, with hand-drawn lettering stacked beside his raised hand in red, yellow and green. Before Lemi Ghariokwu arrived, Fela's sleeves sold the performer: the man, the microphone, the sweat. The lettering already wants to be louder than the photograph.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Gentleman
sleeves.label: EMI
sleeves.artNotes: A monkey's head on a man in a suit, crouched on a black ground flecked with white like static, with the title in a swooping red script. The title track mocks Africans who wear European suits in African heat out of colonial habit; the cover tells the joke in one image. Satire is becoming the house style.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Confusion
sleeves.label: EMI
sleeves.artNotes: A full-colour comic panel: a policeman and a crowd caught in flame-coloured explosions, with the title repeated down the right edge in shifting colours like a sign that can't settle. The record is a commentary on the confused state of post-colonial Lagos, its broken infrastructure and its leadership, and the cover is the gridlock drawn.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Expensive Shit
sleeves.label: Soundworkshop Records
sleeves.artNotes: Fela gives the cover to his people: a photograph of a crowd with raised fists behind barbed wire, under hand-drawn yellow lettering. The title comes from a 1974 arrest: police planted a joint on Fela, he swallowed it, and they held him waiting for the evidence to pass. Legend says he handed over a cellmate's instead.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Zombie
sleeves.label: Coconut (Nigeria); Creole (UK)
sleeves.artNotes: Fela in a pink shirt squares up to soldiers blown up to monstrous size and cut into collage fragments: helmets, hands, boots. The original Coconut sleeve credits the design to Lemi Ghariokwu and the photography to Tunde Kuboye. The record mocks soldiers as zombies who march without thinking; the state's answer was the February 1977 raid on Kalakuta.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Sorrow Tears and Blood
sleeves.label: Kalakuta
sleeves.artNotes: A black-and-white stage photograph of Fela with his saxophone, under a hand-lettered title in white on black. The original Kalakuta sleeve credits the front cover to Okanlawon Banjoko and the photograph to Femi Osunla. Lemi Ghariokwu had painted his own, openly political design inspired by the Soweto uprising; Fela turned it down, and the two fell out for eight years. The song itself describes the raid: everybody run, everybody scatter.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: No Agreement
sleeves.label: Afrodisia
sleeves.artNotes: A painted Fela, bare-chested and immovable, surrounded by pebble-shaped bubbles, each lettered with an idea: Black Consciousness, Total Emancipation, Decolonization, Justice, Freedom, Pan-Africanism. The cover is a manifesto laid out like a map. The American trumpeter Lester Bowie plays on the record.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Shuffering and Shmiling
sleeves.artist: Fela Anikulapo Kuti and the Africa 70
sleeves.label: Coconut
sleeves.artNotes: A crowded painted scene: grinning clerics and worshippers pressed together on the left, a pharaoh-like figure enthroned on the right, and a placard asking "Why not African religion". The song mocks Nigerians who suffer quietly in church and mosque while their leaders prosper.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.
Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Family Planning
sleeves.label: Siky Oluyole Records
sleeves.artNotes: Barrister stands in a patterned agbada and cap while his name runs in tall outlined letters across the top and down the edge of the sleeve, with the full tracklist printed on the front. "Family Planning" opens side one. Here the band is billed as his Progressive Fuji Commanders.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Austerity
sleeves.label: Obey
sleeves.artNotes: A pale sleeve with a framed photograph of Obey in flowing white robes on a grassy bank, the title in a slanting blue script and his billing, Chief Commander Ebenezer Obey and his Inter-Reformers Band, in pink capitals. It came out in 1982, the year the Shagari government's Economic Stabilisation Act cut imports and travel allowances, and its title names the times.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Juju Music
sleeves.artist: King Sunny Adé and His African Beats
sleeves.label: Mango (Island Records)
sleeves.artNotes: A posterised portrait of Adé dissolving into bands of red, gold, green and black, with a small serif title. This was his major-label debut and first worldwide release, produced by Martin Meissonnier.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Opportunity
sleeves.label: Olumo Records
sleeves.artNotes: A painted portrait of a bearded elder in a feathered headdress shares the sleeve with a photograph of De Coque in white, a red cap on his head and a fan in his hand, under the billing "Oliver De Coque and his Expo '76: Ogene Sound Super of Africa". De Coque recorded 93 albums, and his guitar band drew on ogene rhythms and Congolese guitar lines.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Synchro System
sleeves.artist: King Sunny Adé and His African Beats
sleeves.label: Mango / Island
sleeves.artNotes: The whole band laid out on a pale ground in rows of small full-length figures, each in traditional dress and holding an instrument, with the title running in thin lines between the rows. It's the home-market logic of the band as an institution, redrawn for an international sleeve. The album was Adé's first recorded in London and earned the first Grammy nomination for a Nigerian artist.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Je Ka Jo
sleeves.label: Obey (Nigeria); Virgin (UK)
sleeves.artNotes: A tight, smiling portrait of Obey on purple, framed in black with dancing silhouettes in roundels at each corner and his name in a yellow slab with a heavy shadow. Recorded at Decca Studios in Lagos and mixed in London, it was released in Britain by Virgin in 1983, the same year Island released Adé's Synchro System.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Aura
sleeves.artist: King Sunny Adé and His African Beats
sleeves.label: Island
sleeves.artNotes: Adé's head and shoulders inside a glowing blue circle, his name and the title set around the ring like a halo. It was the last of his three releases for Island.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Fuji Garbage
sleeves.label: Siky Oluyole Records
sleeves.artNotes: Barrister in a red shirt and dark glasses stands against vertical rainbow stripes, with FUJI GARBAGE in tall outlined capitals filling the left of the sleeve. It began a run: Fuji Garbage Series II followed the same year and Series III in 1989, turning a career into a catalogue.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Face 2 Face
sleeves.label: Kennis Music
sleeves.artNotes: 2face in a white vest and hat stands against a wall of torn newsprint and graffiti, under a serif masthead of his name. The design is credited to Lemi Ghariokwu, Fela's cover artist of the 1970s, three decades on. The album carried "African Queen" and spread from Nigeria across western and southern Africa.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Jaga Jaga
sleeves.label: Kennis Music
sleeves.artNotes: Abdulkareem in a red top and a beanie stitched with "ED", hands clasped, against a psychedelic blur of colour, with Jaga Jaga in a looping script. The title track's attack on corruption and suffering got it banned from radio and publicly criticised by President Obasanjo, and it became his best-known song.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Get Squared
sleeves.label: Square Records
sleeves.artNotes: The twins in white caps and white outfits point out of a blue swirl. "P-SQUARE" is set in wide, bevelled chrome with "Get Squared" in a flourished script beneath. It is the CD era's chrome lettering at its purest, on the album that gave them "Bizzy Body" and "Temptation".

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: No Long Thing
sleeves.label: Mo' Hits Records
sleeves.artNotes: A grinning close-up of D'banj with his name in a big swooping script. The cover itself advertises "with smash hit single Tongolo", the sticker printed into the design to sell from a market stall. Produced by Don Jazzy.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Expressions
sleeves.label: Astromedia
sleeves.artNotes: The group in dark shirts stand under STYL PLUS in heavy chrome capitals, the title in worn grey lowercase across the bottom: a sober, almost monochrome sleeve for the R&B harmony group whose name is built from its founders' first names.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Game Over
sleeves.label: Square Records
sleeves.artNotes: The twins in white suits fan playing cards at the camera while dice fly out of the frame, a skyline glowing behind them, under a chrome "Game Over". Conceived as a visual album, with a video for nearly every song. A 2008 reissue carries a different cover.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution scan via Discogs, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Curriculum Vitae
sleeves.label: Mo' Hits Records
sleeves.artNotes: The label as a band: D'banj, Wande Coal, Dr SID, D'Prince and K-Switch lined up in white tees and sunglasses, the title in a script inside a gold oval. A compilation released in December 2007 and produced by Don Jazzy.

sleeves.title: Mushin 2 Mo' Hits
sleeves.label: Mo' Hits Records
sleeves.artNotes: Wande Coal in electric-blue sunglasses fills the frame against black, his name in a rounded logotype with "coal" in blue, the M2M monogram and the Mo' Hits shield in the corners. Produced entirely by Don Jazzy, it is often called the most influential Nigerian debut album of all time.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Superstar
sleeves.label: Empire Mates Entertainment
sleeves.artNotes: Wizkid in a red cap and named sunglasses against rainbow light rays and stars, the title in bold pink and white. A debut produced by Samklef, E-Kelly, Shizzi and others, with credits printed on the back cover.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Omo Baba Olowo
sleeves.label: HKN Music
sleeves.artNotes: Davido in a cap and shades under purple stage light, his name in a heavy chrome-edged stencil with the subtitle "The Genesis". The previous decade's gloss lingers on a debut that mixed Afrobeats and hip-hop.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: L.I.F.E
sleeves.label: Aristokrat Records
sleeves.artNotes: A pale, almost empty sleeve: a small photograph of a figure in traditional dress, the title in a looping script, and "Leaving an impact for eternity" spelled out in spaced capitals. Quiet and archival for a debut that sold 40,000 copies on its first day.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Once Upon a Time
sleeves.label: Mavin Records / 323 Entertainment
sleeves.artNotes: Three portraits of Tiwa Savage in white on an off-white seamless ground, her name in widely spaced capitals and the title in a red script. Fashion-editorial restraint, the decade's new cover language.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: Baddest Guy Ever Liveth
sleeves.label: YBNL Nation
sleeves.artNotes: Olamide in a white, toga-like robe with a red sash, arms spread, against a muted studio backdrop, the title in a small script at the top. The king of Yoruba street-hop, cast as an emperor.

sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution image via Wikipedia, shown for commentary.
sleeves.title: King of Queens
sleeves.label: Effyzzie Music Group
sleeves.artNotes: Yemi Alade crowned with a headpiece of gold rays against black, her name in thin display capitals. A studio portrait made to work as a single striking image, on the debut that carried "Johnny".

sleeves.title: Sounds from the Other Side
sleeves.label: Starboy Entertainment / RCA
sleeves.artNotes: A white sleeve with Wizkid's profile, in round sunglasses, set inside a burning orange disc, the title hand-lettered in an arc above it and his name small below. His major-label debut, mostly Caribbean-influenced, won Best R&B/Pop Album at The Headies 2018.

sleeves.title: African Giant
sleeves.label: Spaceship / Bad Habit / Atlantic / Warner
sleeves.artNotes: Burna Boy engraved as the face on a banknote, in sunglasses and a Fela Kuti pendant, with "African Giant" set in banknote lettering across stacked notes. The title answered Coachella's organisers, who had printed his name in a small font on the festival poster.

sleeves.title: Twice as Tall
sleeves.label: Spaceship / Bad Habit / Atlantic / Warner
sleeves.artNotes: Burna Boy as a titan, boot thrust at the viewer, striding a highway past pyramids, the sphinx and West African monuments under a burning sky. Street signs read "Burna" and "Boy", and there's no title anywhere: he let the image speak. A companion comic, The Secret Flame, was narrated by Benson Idonije, who once managed Fela.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Made in Lagos
sleeves.label: Starboy / RCA
sleeves.artNotes: A monochrome portrait: Wizkid in bone-coloured clothes against a matching ground, one hand over his face, the title in a loose handwritten script. An earlier, colourful design packed with Lagos icons (the sun, the traffic, Fela, the Lekki-Ikoyi bridge, the Eyo masquerade) gave way to this near-silent self-portrait. The release was postponed to 30 October because of the #EndSARS protests.

sleeves.title: Rave & Roses
sleeves.label: Jonzing World / Mavin
sleeves.artNotes: A cream page with a story scattered across it: a skeleton running towards a smiling sun with a rose, a burning house, a grave with a sword, a swing hanging from the clouds. Rema sketched the idea, and Lanre Williams finished it in four to five days.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Mr. Money with the Vibe
sleeves.label: YBNL Nation / Empire
sleeves.artNotes: A sepia portrait, gold teeth bared in a grin, mounted in a red frame with the name and title typed on a label strip beneath and the tracklist on a small tag. It reads like a found photograph or an ID card: a debut that introduces its star like a document.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Timeless
sleeves.label: Davido Music Worldwide / Columbia / Sony
sleeves.artNotes: Davido's head in profile, filled with a moonlit savannah: elephants, trees, a path leading to an hourglass, a bird at the top left. He said the elephants, trees and bird honour his late son Ifeanyi, and the hourglass asks listeners for patience. Don Jazzy suggested the title.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.

sleeves.title: Born in the Wild
sleeves.label: Since '93 / RCA
sleeves.artNotes: Tems emerging from total black, light catching only her hair, her face and the silver at her throat and wrists. Almost nothing else is on the cover. It is the decade's restraint at its most extreme: a debut album that trusts a single lit face.
sleeves.imageCredit: Cover art © the rights holders. Low-resolution reference image via Wikipedia (non-free file), shown for commentary.
verify: Photographer (reported as Adrienne Raquel; not confirmed)

sleeves.title: The Year I Turned 21
sleeves.label: Mavin / Republic
sleeves.artNotes: Ayra Starr leaning out of a red vintage car into a burnt-orange sunset, her name in pink script, the title stacked in caps. She described posing against a highway backdrop, leaning on a vintage car, and feeling like "a bag of money". It's one vivid accent, the red of the car, doing all the work.
